claim: Nature has evolved many supramolecular proteins assembled in certain, sometimes even seemingly oversophisticated, morphological manners.
source: Nature has evolved many supramolecular proteins assembled in certain, sometimes even seemingly oversophisticated, morphological manners.
evidence: This is a general statement about protein evolution presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript, but draws on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Only a small portion of proteins function in isolation in cells, whereas the majority is assembled into complexes through protein-protein interactions with identical or different protein subunit(s).
source: Recent studies have evidenced that only a small portion of proteins function in isolation in cells, whereas the majority is assembled into complexes through protein-protein interactions with identical or different protein subunit(s) (Marsh et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Marsh et al., 2013.

claim: Proposals for the advantages associated with a multimeric-units complex instead of a long single polypeptide chain include better error control in synthesis, greater coding and folding efficiency, and possibility of allosteric regulation.
source: proposals for the advantages associated with a multimeric-units complex instead of a long single polypeptide chain include better error control in synthesis, greater coding and folding efficiency, and possibility of allosteric regulation (Goodsell and Olson, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Goodsell and Olson, 2000.

claim: Evolution of dihedral complexes takes place in multiple steps (e.g. C1→C5→D5), in contrast to cyclic complexes which evolve in one step (e.g. C1→C5).
source: In contrast to the cyclic complexes which evolve in one step (e.g. C1→C5), evolution of dihedral complexes takes place in multiple steps (e.g. C1→C5→D5) (Levy et al., 2008), and adds another layer of structural complexity.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Levy et al., 2008.

claim: Glutamine synthetases (GSs) are one of the most ancient functioning enzymes in existence and a central enzyme in nitrogen metabolism of all living organisms.
source: One such an example is glutamine synthetases (GSs) (EC 6.3.1.2), one of the most ancient functioning enzymes in existence and a central enzyme in nitrogen metabolism of all living organisms, catalyzing the formation of glutamine by condensation of glutamate with ammonia using ATP as an energy source (Eisenberg et al., 2000; Stadtman and Ginsburg, 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eisenberg et al., 2000 and Stadtman and Ginsburg, 1974.

claim: GS catalyzes the formation of glutamine by condensation of glutamate with ammonia using ATP as an energy source.
source: One such an example is glutamine synthetases (GSs) (EC 6.3.1.2), one of the most ancient functioning enzymes in existence and a central enzyme in nitrogen metabolism of all living organisms, catalyzing the formation of glutamine by condensation of glutamate with ammonia using ATP as an energy source (Eisenberg et al., 2000; Stadtman and Ginsburg, 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eisenberg et al., 2000 and Stadtman and Ginsburg, 1974.

claim: Three classes of GS enzymes have been identified in different organisms, namely, GSI, GSII, and GSIII.
source: Three classes of GS enzymes have been identified in different organisms, namely, GSI, GSII, and GSIII.
evidence: This is a statement of established classification in the field.

claim: All three classes of GS enzymes, despite dramatic differences in amino acid sequences and protein sizes, share quaternary geometry in dihedral symmetry assembled with two oligomeric rings.
source: Decades of studies have established a striking notion that all three classes of GS enzymes, despite of dramatic differences in amino acid sequences and protein sizes, share quaternary geometry in dihedral symmetry assembled with two oligomeric rings (Brown et al., 1994; van Rooyen et al., 2011; Almassy et al., 1986; Gill and Eisenberg, 2001; Gill et al., 2002; Unno et al., 2006; Torreira et al., 2014; Krajewski et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to Brown et al., 1994; van Rooyen et al., 2011; Almassy et al., 1986; Gill and Eisenberg, 2001; Gill et al., 2002; Unno et al., 2006; Torreira et al., 2014; Krajewski et al., 2008.

claim: The active sites of GS are located at the clefts formed between two neighboring protomers within the same ring and distal to the ring-ring interface.
source: Considering that the active sites of GS are located at the clefts formed between two neighboring protomers within the same ring and distal to the ring-ring interface, each isolated GS subcomplex ring holds multiple integral catalytic sites (Eisenberg et al., 2000; Betti et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eisenberg et al., 2000 and Betti et al., 2012.

claim: Each isolated GS subcomplex ring holds multiple integral catalytic sites.
source: Considering that the active sites of GS are located at the clefts formed between two neighboring protomers within the same ring and distal to the ring-ring interface, each isolated GS subcomplex ring holds multiple integral catalytic sites (Eisenberg et al., 2000; Betti et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eisenberg et al., 2000 and Betti et al., 2012, and is also an inference from the location of active sites.

claim: GSIIs from Camellia sinensis (CsGSIb) and Glycine max (GmGSβ2) share an overall very high sequence homology (~90% identical and ~97% conserved).
source: Primary structure analysis reveals GSIIs from the plants of Camellia sinensis (CsGSIb) and Glycine max (GmGSβ2) share an overall very high sequence homology (~90 % identical and ~97 % conserved) and absolutely conserved substrate-binding and catalytic sites (Figure 1a)
evidence: This claim is supported by primary structure analysis presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: CsGSIb and GmGSβ2 have absolutely conserved substrate-binding and catalytic sites.
source: Primary structure analysis reveals GSIIs from the plants of Camellia sinensis (CsGSIb) and Glycine max (GmGSβ2) share an overall very high sequence homology (~90 % identical and ~97 % conserved) and absolutely conserved substrate-binding and catalytic sites (Figure 1a)
evidence: This claim is supported by primary structure analysis presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: A significant portion of amino acid variations between CsGSIb and GmGSβ2 are clustered at the interface between two pentamer rings.
source: with, however, a significant portion of amino acid variations clustered at the interface between two pentamer rings (Figure 1a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1a and b.

claim: GmGSβ2 is largely a homogeneous decamer in solution.
source: MALS analysis shows the GSII from Glycine max being largely a homogeneous decamer in solution (Figure 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by MALS experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The majority fraction (~82%) of CsGSIb adopts a pentameric configuration, along with a minor fraction (~18%) being decameric.
source: In contrast, under the same condition the majority fraction (~82%) of CsGSIb adopts a pentameric configuration, along with a minor fraction (~18%) being decameric (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by MALS experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: CsGSIb exists in pentamer-decamer dynamic equilibrium in solution.
source: We further show that CsGSIb exists in pentamer-decamer dynamic equilibrium in solution and a mixture of electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions is responsible for attaching of two pentameric rings; whereas substrates or ligands show no appreciable effect on the decamer-forming properties (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A mixture of electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions is responsible for attaching of two pentameric rings in CsGSIb.
source: We further show that CsGSIb exists in pentamer-decamer dynamic equilibrium in solution and a mixture of electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions is responsible for attaching of two pentameric rings; whereas substrates or ligands show no appreciable effect on the decamer-forming properties (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Substrates or ligands show no appreciable effect on the decamer-forming properties of CsGSIb.
source: We further show that CsGSIb exists in pentamer-decamer dynamic equilibrium in solution and a mixture of electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions is responsible for attaching of two pentameric rings; whereas substrates or ligands show no appreciable effect on the decamer-forming properties (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: GmGSβ2 forms homogeneous, double stacked-ring shaped particles.
source: Two-dimensional (2D) class averages revealed that GmGSβ2 forms homogeneous, double stacked-ring shaped particles (Figure 1e), in line with the decameric organization pattern previously reported for other GSII species (Unno et al., 2006; Torreira et al., 2014; Krajewski et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by negative-stain EM data shown in Figure 1e and is consistent with previous reports cited.

claim: CsGSIb adopts a mixture of two quaternary structural modes: detached pentamers and decamers composed of two stacked pentamer rings.
source: In contrast, CsGSIb adopted a mixture of two quaternary structural modes: detached pentamers (Figure 1f) and decamers composed of two stacked pentamer rings (Figure 1g), consistent with the above MALS analysis result (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by negative-stain EM data shown in Figure 1f and 1g, and is consistent with MALS data in Figure 1d.

claim: CsGSIb demonstrates two species in solution with molecular weights of 191 kDa and 395 kDa, corresponding to the pentameric and decameric configurations, respectively.
source: Analytical ultracentrifugation (AUC) was carried out to quantitively assess the thermodynamic parameters of CsGSIb pentamer-decamer transition, which demonstrated two species for CsGSIb in solution with molecular weights of 191 kDa and 395 kDa (Figure 2a), corresponding to the pentameric and decameric configurations, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by AUC experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The pentamer-pentamer dissociation constant (Kd) of CsGSIb is 0.27 ± 0.06 μM at room temperature.
source: Sedimentation profiles at various protein concentrations were analyzed and a global analysis of the data yielded a pentamer-pentamer dissociation constant (Kd) of 0.27 ± 0.06 μM at room temperature.
evidence: This claim is supported by AUC experimental data analysis.

claim: The dissociation constant within the sub-micromolar range allows CsGSIb to predominantly exist as isolated pentamers under the concentration assayed for enzymatic activities.
source: It is noteworthy that the dissociation constant within the sub-micromolar range allows CsGSIb to predominantly exist as isolated pentamers under the concentration assayed for enzymatic activities, laying a solid foundation for further probing the functional role of the decamer formation in modulating the enzyme activity of GS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured dissociation constant and its implications for the experimental conditions.

claim: GmGSβ2 demonstrates significant GS activities when supplied with ammonium chloride.
source: As shown in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, when supplied with ammonium chloride, the stable decamer-adopting GmGSβ2 demonstrated significant GS activities.
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic activity assay data shown in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: GmGSβ2 has turnover numbers (kcat) of ~12.8 min–1 and Michaelis constants (Km) of ~44 μM.
source: Further steady-state kinetic measurements yielded turnover numbers (kcat) and Michaelis constants (Km) of ~12.8 min–1 and ~44 μM, respectively (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by steady-state kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: CsGSIb only demonstrates basal activity.
source: In sharp contrast, CsGSIb only demonstrated basal activity (Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a), consistent with previous observations that the isolated single-ringed GSII species is nonfunctional (Llorca et al., 2006; Mäck, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic activity assay data shown in Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, and is consistent with previous reports cited.

claim: The isolated single-ringed GSII species is nonfunctional.
source: In sharp contrast, CsGSIb only demonstrated basal activity (Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a), consistent with previous observations that the isolated single-ringed GSII species is nonfunctional (Llorca et al., 2006; Mäck, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Llorca et al., 2006 and Mäck, 1998.

claim: Five times increase in the concentration of CsGSIb assayed (from 1 μM to 5 μM) resulted in ~30 folds increase in activity, displaying a significant concentration-dependent simulation effect.
source: Indeed, five times increase in the concentration of CsGSIb assayed (from 1 μM to 5 μM) resulted in ~30 folds increase in activity, that is ~6 folds activity increase per unit of enzyme, displaying a significant concentration-dependent simulation effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic activity assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The mutation I143L in CsGSIb led to a drastic shift in the oligomerization equilibrium towards decamer assembly, causing significant increase in the distribution of decameric state from ~18% in the WT-CsGSIb to >95%.
source: SEC-MALS measurements revealed both mutations of I143L and EVK138DIQ led to a drastic shift in the oligomerization equilibrium towards decamer assembly (Figure 2d and f), causing significant increase in the distribution of decameric state from ~18 % in the WT-CsGSIb (Figure 1d) to >95% and ~ 72%, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC-MALS experimental data shown in Figure 2d and comparison with Figure 1d.

claim: The mutation EVK138DIQ in CsGSIb led to a drastic shift in the oligomerization equilibrium towards decamer assembly, causing significant increase in the distribution of decameric state from ~18% in the WT-CsGSIb to ~72%.
source: SEC-MALS measurements revealed both mutations of I143L and EVK138DIQ led to a drastic shift in the oligomerization equilibrium towards decamer assembly (Figure 2d and f), causing significant increase in the distribution of decameric state from ~18 % in the WT-CsGSIb (Figure 1d) to >95% and ~ 72%, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC-MALS experimental data shown in Figure 2f and comparison with Figure 1d.

claim: Substitution of the tyrosine at the residue 150 with a phenylalanine showed no appreciable change in CsGSIb quaternary organization mode.
source: In contrast, substitution of the tyrosine at the residue 150 with a phenylalanine showed no appreciable change in its quaternary organization mode (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a), suggesting no critical role for the residue Y150 in maintaining two CsGSIb pentameric ring subcomplexes attached.
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC-MALS experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Residue Y150 has no critical role in maintaining two CsGSIb pentameric ring subcomplexes attached.
source: In contrast, substitution of the tyrosine at the residue 150 with a phenylalanine showed no appreciable change in its quaternary organization mode (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a), suggesting no critical role for the residue Y150 in maintaining two CsGSIb pentameric ring subcomplexes attached.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of effect of the Y150F mutation on quaternary structure.

claim: Replacement of I143 or EVK at residues 138–140 with leucine or DIQ yielded ring-ring disassociation constants of ~0.01 or ~0.04 μM, respectively.
source: Further AUC analysis revealed replacement of I143 or EVK at residues 138–140 with leucine or DIQ yielded ring-ring disassociation constants of ~0.01 or ~ 0.04 μM, respectively (Figure 2e and g), that is, ~ 27 or ~ 7 folds of increase in the ring-ring binding affinity compared with that of WT-CsGSIb.
evidence: This claim is supported by AUC experimental data shown in Figure 2e and g.

claim: The mutations I143L and EVK138DIQ resulted in ~27 or ~7 folds of increase in the ring-ring binding affinity compared with that of WT-CsGSIb.
source: Further AUC analysis revealed replacement of I143 or EVK at residues 138–140 with leucine or DIQ yielded ring-ring disassociation constants of ~0.01 or ~ 0.04 μM, respectively (Figure 2e and g), that is, ~ 27 or ~ 7 folds of increase in the ring-ring binding affinity compared with that of WT-CsGSIb.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured dissociation constants.

claim: The Gibbs energy changes upon mutation (ΔΔG) for I143L and EVK138DIQ were calculated to be –8.1 kJ/mol and –4.7 kJ/mol, respectively.
source: The Gibbs energy changes upon mutation (ΔΔG) for I143L and EVK138DIQ were calculated to be –8.1 kJ/mol and –4.7 kJ/mol, respectively.
evidence: This is a calculation based on thermodynamic data.

claim: Both mutations of I143L and EVK138DIQ caused dramatic increase in catalytic activity of CsGSIb of ~76 and ~64 folds, respectively.
source: As shown in Figure 2h–j, both mutations of I143L and EVK138DIQ caused dramatic increase in catalytic activity of ~76 and ~ 64 folds, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic activity assay data shown in Figure 2h–j.

claim: All mutated amino acids are distal to either the catalytic site or substrate binding regions with distances > 20 Å.
source: As all mutated amino acids are distal to either the catalytic site or substrate binding regions with distances > 20 Å and hence are unlikely to be directly involved in catalytic reaction, we infer that the stimulations of the enzymatic activity of CsGSIb upon residue perturbations are induced by remote contacts between two pentamer rings.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the protein.

claim: The stimulations of the enzymatic activity of CsGSIb upon residue perturbations are induced by remote contacts between two pentamer rings.
source: As all mutated amino acids are distal to either the catalytic site or substrate binding regions with distances > 20 Å and hence are unlikely to be directly involved in catalytic reaction, we infer that the stimulations of the enzymatic activity of CsGSIb upon residue perturbations are induced by remote contacts between two pentamer rings.
evidence: This is an inference based on the location of mutations and their effects on activity.

claim: The mutation of Y150F did not alter pentamer-decamer equilibrium of CsGSIb and showed no noticeable change in enzymatic activity.
source: As expected, the mutation of Y150F, which did not alter pentamer-decamer equilibrium of CsGSIb, showed no noticeable change in enzymatic activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic activity assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b.

claim: GmGSβ2 and CsGSIbDec are arranged in D5 symmetry with two pentameric rings stacked in a head-to-head manner.
source: 3D classifications of 104,717 and 43,876 particles for GmGSβ2 and CsGSIbDec, respectively, revealed that both molecules were arranged in D5 symmetry with two pentameric rings stacked in a head-to-head manner (Figure 3a–b), a strikingly conserved structural feature for type II GS species (Unno et al., 2006; Torreira et al., 2014; Krajewski et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 3a–b and is consistent with previous reports cited.

claim: Refinement of the GmGSβ2 and CsGSIbDec structures yielded maps with an average resolution of 2.9 Å and 3.3 Å, respectively.
source: Refinement of the GmGSβ2 and CsGSIbDec structures yielded maps with an average resolution of 2.9 Å and 3.3 Å, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3), with literally identical dimensions of 115 Å x 115 Å x 95 Å.
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM structure determination data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: Decamer structures of GmGSβ2 and CsGSIbDec are strikingly similar to each other, as well as to that of the GSII of maize, as highlighted by the root-mean-square deviation (r.m.s.d.) of 0.66–0.80 Å for 328–352 aligned Cα atoms.
source: As expected from the very high conservation in amino acid sequence (Figure 1a), decamer structures of GmGSβ2 and CsGSIbDec are strikingly similar to each other, as well as to that of the GSII of maize (pdb accession number 2D3A), as highlighted by the root-mean-square deviation (r.m.s.d.) of 0.66–0.80 Å for 328–352 aligned Cα atoms.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison analysis of cryo-EM structures.

claim: The active sites of GmGSβ2, CsGSIbDec are structurally highly similar to each other, as well as to that of the maize GSII.
source: The active sites of GmGSβ2, CsGSIbDec are structurally highly similar to each other, as well as to that of the maize GSII (Figure 3c), suggesting the catalysis mechanisms of these plant GSIIs are essentially identical.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The catalysis mechanisms of GmGSβ2, CsGSIbDec, and maize GSII are essentially identical.
source: The active sites of GmGSβ2, CsGSIbDec are structurally highly similar to each other, as well as to that of the maize GSII (Figure 3c), suggesting the catalysis mechanisms of these plant GSIIs are essentially identical.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural similarity of active sites.

claim: Structural alignments of GSs reveals a conservative catalytic site geometry across a wide range of species.
source: Indeed, structural alignments of GSs reveals a conservative catalytic site geometry across a wide range of species (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural alignment data presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The overall buried inter-ring surfaces for both GmGSβ2 and CsGSIbDec amount to ~2000 Å2, that is approximately only 400 Å2 per individual monomer–monomer interaction.
source: The overall buried inter-ring surfaces for both GmGSβ2 and CsGSIbDec amount to ~2000 Å2, that is approximately only 400 Å2 per individual monomer–monomer interaction.
evidence: This is a calculation based on structural analysis.

claim: The small buried inter-ring surface area highlights the weakness of the inter-ring contacts, characteristic of type II GS.
source: This highlights the weakness of the inter-ring contacts, characteristic of type II GS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the calculated buried surface area.

claim: In both GmGSβ2 and CsGSIbDec structures, the inter-ring contacts are established by only a limited number of hydrophobic and polar interactions provided by the residues 136–141 and 146–152 segments of each of the intervening subunits.
source: Indeed, in both structures the inter-ring contacts are established by only a limited number of hydrophobic and polar interactions provided by the residues 136–141 and 146–152 segments of each of the intervening subunits (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), which behave as two gear teeth (thereafter named as tooth-1 and tooth-2, respectively) interlocking the two pentameric rings (Figure 3d–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and Figure 3d–f.

claim: The residues 136–141 and 146–152 segments behave as two gear teeth (tooth-1 and tooth-2, respectively) interlocking the two pentameric rings.
source: Indeed, in both structures the inter-ring contacts are established by only a limited number of hydrophobic and polar interactions provided by the residues 136–141 and 146–152 segments of each of the intervening subunits (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), which behave as two gear teeth (thereafter named as tooth-1 and tooth-2, respectively) interlocking the two pentameric rings (Figure 3d–f).
evidence: This is a description based on structural analysis shown in Figure 3d–f.

claim: The local structure of the teeth regions that mediate inter-ring interactions remains largely the same in GmGSβ2 and CsGSIbDec.
source: Intriguingly, the local structure of the teeth regions that mediate inter-ring interactions remains largely the same in GmGSβ2 and CsGSIbDec (Figure 3d–e), suggesting the dramatically different propensities of GmGSβ2 and CsGSIb for decamer formation are due to the nature of the amino acids involved in inter-ring contacts, rather than the structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3d–e.

claim: The dramatically different propensities of GmGSβ2 and CsGSIb for decamer formation are due to the nature of the amino acids involved in inter-ring contacts, rather than the structure.
source: Intriguingly, the local structure of the teeth regions that mediate inter-ring interactions remains largely the same in GmGSβ2 and CsGSIbDec (Figure 3d–e), suggesting the dramatically different propensities of GmGSβ2 and CsGSIb for decamer formation are due to the nature of the amino acids involved in inter-ring contacts, rather than the structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural similarity despite different oligomerization propensities.

claim: Replacement of I143 with leucine may stabilize the conformation of tooth-1 via its interaction with the residue of L134, thus playing an important role in stabilizing decamer architecture.
source: Although the residue of I143 is not directly involved in inter-ring contact, we argue that its replacement with leucine may stabilize the conformation of tooth-1 via its interaction with the residue of L134, thus playing an important role in stabilizing decamer architecture (Figure 2d and e).
evidence: This is speculation based on structural analysis and mutation effects shown in Figure 2d and e.

claim: CsGSIbPen exhibited high conformational heterogeneity and 3D particles classification generated three similar structures with the r.m.s.d. ranging from 0.6 to 0.8 Å, differing in a few peripheral regions.
source: Unexpected, CsGSIbPen exhibited high conformational heterogeneity and 3D particles classification generated three similar structures with the r.m.s.d. ranging from 0.6 to 0.8 Å, differing in a few peripheral regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM structure determination data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Several regions are missing in the electron density map of all three classifications of CsGSIbPen particles, with only 229–255 out of 356 residues electron densities in presence.
source: The most striking difference between CsGSIbPen and CsGSIbDec is that several regions are missing in the electron density map of all three classifications of CsGSIbPen particles, with only 229–255 out of 356 residues electron densities in presence.
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM structure analysis.

claim: CsGSIbPen demonstrated a decagram-shaped density map with a few regions missing at the rim, in sharp contrast to a pentagon-shaped map yielded by the CsGSIbDec particles.
source: As a result, CsGSIbPen demonstrated a decagram-shaped density map with a few regions missing at the rim (Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a), in sharp contrast to a pentagon-shaped map yielded by the CsGSIbDec particles (Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM density map analysis shown in Figure 4a, 4b, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: For the 229–255 residues that show clear density in CsGSIbPen particles, the conformation of each subunit in three CsGSIbPen EM structures, as well as the arrangement pattern, closely resembles that of the CsGSIbDec, as evidenced by r.m.s.d. in the range of 0.7–1.0 Å.
source: For the 229–255 residues that show clear density in CsGSIbPen particles, the conformation of each subunit in three CsGSIbPen EM structures, as well as the arrangement pattern, closely resembles that of the CsGSIbDec, as evidenced by r.m.s.d. in the range of 0.7–1.0 Å (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b-d).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b-d.

claim: The density-missing regions include the segments around residues of 110–117, 140–166, and 260–334.
source: The density-missing regions include the segments around residues of 110–117, 140–166, and 260–334, among which, the fragment around residues 260–334 is a major component making up an integral catalytic site (Figure 4c), while the segment of residues 140–166 comprising of the two gear teeth is responsible for ring-ring interaction (Figures 3d–f ,–4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4c and 4d.

claim: The fragment around residues 260–334 is a major component making up an integral catalytic site.
source: The density-missing regions include the segments around residues of 110–117, 140–166, and 260–334, among which, the fragment around residues 260–334 is a major component making up an integral catalytic site (Figure 4c), while the segment of residues 140–166 comprising of the two gear teeth is responsible for ring-ring interaction (Figures 3d–f ,–4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The segment of residues 140–166 comprising of the two gear teeth is responsible for ring-ring interaction.
source: The density-missing regions include the segments around residues of 110–117, 140–166, and 260–334, among which, the fragment around residues 260–334 is a major component making up an integral catalytic site (Figure 4c), while the segment of residues 140–166 comprising of the two gear teeth is responsible for ring-ring interaction (Figures 3d–f ,–4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figures 3d–f and 4d.

claim: Electron density missing often reflects the conformational heterogeneity arising from internal motions.
source: As electron density missing often reflects the conformational heterogeneity arising from internal motions Armache and Cheng, 2019, these observation strongly suggest that the conformation of CsGSIbPen active site is highly dynamic, contrasting sharply to the conformationally largely homogeneous CsGSIbDec.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Armache and Cheng, 2019.

claim: The conformation of CsGSIbPen active site is highly dynamic, contrasting sharply to the conformationally largely homogeneous CsGSIbDec.
source: As electron density missing often reflects the conformational heterogeneity arising from internal motions Armache and Cheng, 2019, these observation strongly suggest that the conformation of CsGSIbPen active site is highly dynamic, contrasting sharply to the conformationally largely homogeneous CsGSIbDec.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electron density missing in CsGSIbPen structures.

claim: Thermal shift assays show the melting temperature (Tm) of wild-type CsGSIb is significantly lower than that of its mutants of I143L or EVK138DIQ, indicating structural instability for the pentameric GSII.
source: In support this, thermal shift assays show the melting temperature (Tm) of wild-type CsGSIb is significantly lower than that of its mutants of I143L or EVK138DIQ, indicating of structural instability for the pentameric GSII (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by thermal shift assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The dramatically difference in the dynamic property of catalytic sites accounts for the distinct activities of pentameric and decameric CsGSIb.
source: We therefore conclude that the dramatically difference in the dynamic property of catalytic sites accounts for the distinct activities of pentameric and decameric CsGSIb.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural and activity data presented.

claim: 14-3-3 proteins are an important family of scaffold proteins that bind and regulate many key proteins involved in diverse intracellular processes in all eukaryotic organisms.
source: 14-3-3 proteins are an important family of scaffold proteins that bind and regulate many key proteins involved in diverse intracellular processes in all eukaryotic organisms (Tzivion et al., 2001; Chevalier et al., 2009; Obsilova and Obsil, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tzivion et al., 2001; Chevalier et al., 2009; Obsilova and Obsil, 2020.

claim: Self-dimerization of 14-3-3 proteins, which induces dimerization of their clients, plays a key role in its functional scaffolding and subsequent activity regulation.
source: In particular, self-dimerization of 14-3-3 proteins, which induces dimerization of their clients, plays a key role in its functional scaffolding and subsequent activity regulation (Tzivion et al., 2001; Chevalier et al., 2009; Kondo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tzivion et al., 2001; Chevalier et al., 2009; Kondo et al., 2019.

claim: 14-3-3 proteins act as an activator of GSs in various plants.
source: It has been reported that 14-3-3 proteins act as an activator of GSs in various plants (Finnemann and Schjoerring, 2000; Pozuelo et al., 2001; Lima et al., 2006; Riedel et al., 2001), although the detailed activation mechanism remains unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Finnemann and Schjoerring, 2000; Pozuelo et al., 2001; Lima et al., 2006; Riedel et al., 2001.

claim: The GS from Medicago truncatula, whose activity is simulated upon binding to 14-3-3 protein, has been shown to exhibit a dynamic pentamer-decamer transition.
source: In support of this, the GS from Medicago truncatula, whose activity is simulated upon binding to 14-3-3 protein (Lima et al., 2006), has been shown to exhibit a dynamic pentamer-decamer transition (Torreira et al., 2014), similar to the CsGSIb presented here (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lima et al., 2006 and Torreira et al., 2014.

claim: Only the higher order complex of tobacco GS-2 that is bound to 14-3-3 is catalytically active.
source: Moreover, it has been shown that only the higher order complex of tobacco GS-2 that is bound to 14-3-3 is catalytically active (Riedel et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Riedel et al., 2001.

claim: Cs14-3-3-1a and Cs14-3-3-1b genes displayed expression patterns highly similar to CsGSI genes.
source: Analysis of their coding genes' expression patterns in tea plant tissues and in nitrogen assimilation or metabolism-related processes allowed us to identify Cs14-3-3-1a and Cs14-3-3-1b genes that displayed expression patterns highly similar to CsGSI genes (Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis data shown in Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The expression levels of Cs14-3-3-1a and Cs14-3-3-1b genes were regulated upon changes in the availability of ammonia.
source: Moreover, the expression levels of Cs14-3-3-1a and Cs14-3-3-1b genes were regulated upon changes in the availability of ammonia (Figure 5b and c), the substrate of GS, suggesting both Cs14-3-3-1a and Cs14-3-3-1b are physiologically related to GS.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis data shown in Figure 5b and c.

claim: Both Cs14-3-3-1a and Cs14-3-3-1b are physiologically related to GS.
source: Moreover, the expression levels of Cs14-3-3-1a and Cs14-3-3-1b genes were regulated upon changes in the availability of ammonia (Figure 5b and c), the substrate of GS, suggesting both Cs14-3-3-1a and Cs14-3-3-1b are physiologically related to GS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the co-regulation of gene expression with ammonia availability.

claim: Cs14-3-3-1a and 1b could self-dimerize or form heterodimers in plant cells.
source: As expected, Cs14-3-3-1a and 1b could self-dimerize or form heterodimers in plant cells (Figure 5e), consistent with 14-3-3 scaffold proteins adopting a dimeric structure (Tzivion et al., 2001; Chevalier et al., 2009; Kondo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by BiFC assay data shown in Figure 5e and is consistent with previous reports cited.

claim: Formation of the fluorescent complex clearly demonstrated the interaction of Cs14-3-3-1a with CsGSIb.
source: Importantly, formation of the fluorescent complex clearly demonstrated the interaction of Cs14-3-3-1a with CsGSIb (Figure 5f).
evidence: This claim is supported by BiFC assay data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Along with the reduction in Cs14-3-3-1a transcript level, the glutamine contents, as well as the crude enzyme activity, were drastically reduced.
source: We show that, along with the reduction in Cs14-3-3-1a transcript level, the glutamine contents (Figure 5i), as well as the crude enzyme activity (Figure 5j), were drastically reduced, indicating the 14-3-3 protein in Camellia sinensis functions as an activator molecule of CsGSIb.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi knockdown experiment data shown in Figure 5i and 5j.

claim: The 14-3-3 protein in Camellia sinensis functions as an activator molecule of CsGSIb.
source: We show that, along with the reduction in Cs14-3-3-1a transcript level, the glutamine contents (Figure 5i), as well as the crude enzyme activity (Figure 5j), were drastically reduced, indicating the 14-3-3 protein in Camellia sinensis functions as an activator molecule of CsGSIb.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RNAi knockdown experiment results.

claim: The active sites within isolated CsGSIbPen rings are highly disordered and the unstable catalytic environments render it catalytically inactive.
source: Taken together, our cryo-EM structures allow us to propose a disorder-order transition mechanism of how the GSII activity is regulated by changes in oligomeric state: (1) The active sites within isolated CsGSIbPen rings are highly disordered and the unstable catalytic environments render it catalytically inactive
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the cryo-EM structural data.

claim: Upon stacking of two pentameric rings and formation of a decamer, the signals of interactions mediated by the gear teeth of each intervening subunit are propagated to the active sites and induce folding, which, in turn, unlock the catalytic potential of GSII.
source: (2) Upon stacking of two pentameric rings and formation of a decamer, the signals of interactions mediated by the gear teeth of each intervening subunit are propagated to the active sites and induce folding, which, in turn, unlock the catalytic potential of GSII (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the cryo-EM structural data and shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The dynamic association-disassociation of GSII subcomplexes have been widely observed in various species including humans, plants other than Camellia sinensis, and fungi.
source: Indeed, the dynamic association-disassociation of GSII subcomplexes, a prerequisite for this modulatory machinery, have been widely observed in various species including humans (Denman and Wedler, 1984), plants other than Camellia sinensis reported here (Torreira et al., 2014; Llorca et al., 2006) and fungi (Mora, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Denman and Wedler, 1984; Torreira et al., 2014; Llorca et al., 2006; and Mora, 1990.

claim: The activation mechanism shown here may represent a general regulatory machinery harnessed by many eukaryotes to ensure optimal utilization of nitrogen sources.
source: Therefore, the activation mechamism shown here may represent a general regulatory machinery harnessed by many eukaryotes to ensure optimal utilization of nitrogen sources, and the infrastructure of fragile ring-ring contacts evolutionarily chosen by many eukaryotes offers a convenient and robust avenue for activity regulation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings and their potential generalizability.

claim: The infrastructure of fragile ring-ring contacts evolutionarily chosen by many eukaryotes offers a convenient and robust avenue for activity regulation.
source: Therefore, the activation mechamism shown here may represent a general regulatory machinery harnessed by many eukaryotes to ensure optimal utilization of nitrogen sources, and the infrastructure of fragile ring-ring contacts evolutionarily chosen by many eukaryotes offers a convenient and robust avenue for activity regulation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings and their potential evolutionary significance.

claim: Inhibition of the GS in Mycobacterium tuberculosis has long been recognized as a novel antibiotic strategy to treat tuberculosis.
source: For example, inhibition of the GS in Mycobacterium tuberculosis has long been recognized as a novel antibiotic strategy to treat tuberculosis (Harth and Horwitz, 2003; Gising et al., 2012; Kumari and Subbarao, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Harth and Horwitz, 2003; Gising et al., 2012; Kumari and Subbarao, 2020.

claim: The overall geometry of the active site is the most conserved structural element amongst GS enzymes.
source: However, because the overall geometry of the active site is the most conserved structural element amongst GS enzymes (Eisenberg et al., 2000; van Rooyen et al., 2011; Unno et al., 2006), the traditional strategy of selective inhibition, which relies heavily on the subtle difference in the active sites from different species, has only achieved limited success.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eisenberg et al., 2000; van Rooyen et al., 2011; Unno et al., 2006.

claim: The traditional strategy of selective inhibition of GS, which relies heavily on the subtle difference in the active sites from different species, has only achieved limited success.
source: However, because the overall geometry of the active site is the most conserved structural element amongst GS enzymes (Eisenberg et al., 2000; van Rooyen et al., 2011; Unno et al., 2006), the traditional strategy of selective inhibition, which relies heavily on the subtle difference in the active sites from different species, has only achieved limited success.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current drug design strategies.

claim: Overexpression of GS has been investigated extensively for decades with the goal of improving crop nitrogen use efficiency, but the outcome has not been consistent.
source: Moreover, although overexpression of GS has been investigated extensively for decades with the goal of improving crop nitrogen use efficiency, the outcome has not been consistent (Thomsen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thomsen et al., 2014.
